query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the conventional high‐heat additive manufacturing regime with a friction stir deposition (FSD) process for AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will overcome residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity by eliminating melting, thereby inducing severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization that refines the microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock produced (via mechanical alloying) in a near-spherical morphology with controlled particle size distribution suitable for additive deposition.
generation.intervention: Process the feedstock using an additive friction stir deposition (FSD) method instead of a fusion‐based method.
generation.conditions: Fabricate miniature components (e.g., features <5 mm thick) using tool rotational and traverse speeds optimized to maintain a solid-state (non-melted) process with moderate heat input; processing is carried out at ambient or slightly elevated substrate temperatures to control dynamic recrystallization without reaching melting temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined equiaxed grain structure generated by the severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization inherent in FSD, which minimizes thermal gradients and eliminates solidification defects.
generation.mechanism: Using FSD avoids the high thermal gradients associated with melting and solidification, thereby preventing the generation of high tensile residual stresses. The severe plastic deformation from the rotating tool promotes immediate nucleation resulting in a fine, homogeneous microstructure and reduced dislocation accumulation. This in turn improves mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) and reduces processing complexity (e.g., eliminating the need for inert gas environments or complex thermal management).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to components made by conventional high-thermal-load AM (e.g., laser powder bed fusion), the FSD-processed parts are predicted to have substantially lower residual stresses (potentially a reduction exceeding 50%), improved mechanical performance due to a refined microstructure, and simplified process control.
generation.baseline: Miniature AlCrFeNiSi components manufactured using conventional fusion-based additive manufacturing regimes that typically experience high thermal stresses, degraded microstructures, and complex post-processing requirements.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected to hold for miniature components (feature sizes <5 mm) under conditions where the FSD tool can adequately control heat input; at larger scales or if process parameters are not optimized for the AlCrFeNiSi alloy, thermal accumulation and suboptimal deformation may limit the improvements.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extrapolates from evidence in aluminum alloys processed by AFSD (PMC11277587::web::002::1_introduction) and from studies showing post-process heat treatments optimize high-entropy alloy properties (PMC12113129::web::001::abstract). While the predicted mechanisms are physically sound, the exact window of process parameters and magnitude of improvements for AlCrFeNiSi remain to be experimentally established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a set of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components using both conventional high-thermal-load AM (e.g., laser-based methods) and the proposed FSD process under otherwise comparable geometrical and environmental conditions. Ensure identical feedstock and build geometries. Characterize both sets of components.
measurements: Residual stress mapping via X-ray diffraction
Grain structure and recrystallization assessment via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)
Microstructural defect evaluation (e.g., porosity, cracking) using microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FSD-processed components do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., less than 40% reduction) in residual stresses relative to the conventional AM baseline, or if the mechanical properties (strength and ductility) are not maintained or improved, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) offers unique advantages over other additive manufacturing (AM) processes. It is capable of fabricating large structures due to its high deposition rate [,]. Furthermore, the only consumable is the feedstock material, and no inert gas is necessary for processing aluminium, thus presenting high cost effectiveness and reduced environmental impact of equipment operation [,]. The layer-by-layer solid-state AFSD process allows for flexibility in structure design and the use of wrought aluminium alloy feedstock [], which, in fusion processes, experiences solidification cracking and deformation due to thermal-gradient-induced residual stresses and Scheil solidification [,]. Research on AFSD is mainly focused on Al alloys, although it has also been successfully applied to a broad range of materials such as Ti alloys [,], Mg alloys [], Cu [], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [,], stainless steel [,], and high-tensile steel []. By avoiding the liquification and solidification of the material, AFSD avoids element loss [], porosity [], and cracking [], which are known to occur in fusion AM processes.
